speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO ARRESTING OF DUTCH ELM DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked me whether the department was making any progress in finding a means of arresting Dutch elm disease. I replied that I had no up to the minute information but would take the question as notice.
I am pleased to advise as follows. The Dutch elm disease occurs widely in Ontario and Quebec and in the upper Saint John river valley area of New Brunswick. The causal fungus is carried from diseased trees to healthy ones by bark beetles. Spread of the disease can be reduced by sanitation programs to remove weakened elm trees and branches in which the beetles breed, by spraying with d.d.t. to prevent the entry of beetles into healthy trees, and by prompt felling of diseased elms, with destruction of the bark, to prevent emergence of fungusladen beetles. An effective control program may require use of all three lines of action.
The Department of Forestry carries out continuing insect and disease surveys, and keeps municipalities and the public informed of areas of known distribution of the Dutch elm disease. The department is conducting research on host-parasite relationships as an aid to formulation of improved control procedures. It also provides a diagnostic service so that occurrence of the disease in suspect trees may be confirmed before expensive felling operations are undertaken.
Responsibility for the application of control measures rests with the owners, usually

municipalities or private citizens. The department provides information and advice to such owners on the organization of control procedures.
This is a disease of foreign origin and as such comes under quarantine regulations administered by the plant protection division of the Department of Agriculture. Officers of my department co-operate fully with the plant protection division in the exchange of information leading to appropriate quarantine regulations. In the event the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate does not have publication No. 1010 on Dutch elm disease, I am sending him a copy.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing the supplementary budget on the evening of December 20, 1960, I made the

Tariff Board Act
following reference to the subject matter of the resolution now before the committee, as reported at page 1013 of Hansard:
In view of the heavy program of important work which awaits the tariff board, the government proposes to enlarge the board and to provide for expediting its work. The government is fully aware of the urgent need to modernize sectors of the tariff which have become out of date. At the same time we consider it important to provide for careful investigation and public hearings before major tariff revisions are introduced. This permits all interests and all points of view to receive full consideration. We believe that the tariff board is the appropriate body to undertake this task, and that in order to do so expeditiously the board should be enlarged sufficiently to permit it to adopt a panel system.
Accordingly I am placing on the order paper a resolution looking toward a bill which will provide for an increase in the board's membership from five to seven. Additional membership will make it practicable for the board to operate normally as two separate panels, and to proceed simultaneously with two inquiries or appeals. In addition to authorizing an increase in the membership of the board, the bill will provide also for consequential amendments designed to facilitate the adoption and operation of a panel system.
The bill to be introduced pursuant to this resolution, when adopted, will accordingly provide for an increase from five to seven in the number of members of the tariff board. The increase in membership is proposed in order to facilitate the operations of the board. It will enable the board to sit at the same time in two panels, each with a minimum of three members. This change should permit the important functions performed by the board to be discharged more expeditiously, while at the same time ensuring that adequate account is taken of all relevant considerations.
Having regard to the nature of the problems with which the tariff board deals, I think it will be agreed that it is important that each panel be large enough to reflect the possibility of differing points of view. For this reason it has not seemed appropriate for the tariff board to operate with one-man or two-man panels, although such panels may be perfectly satisfactory in some other fields. There would be serious objections, I take it, to having even a two-man panel deal with an important tariff board reference or appeal.
It is contemplated that in future the board will normally sit in two panels, one presided over by the chairman and the other by the first vice chairman. The amendments to the act which are proposed will not, however, restrict the wide measure of freedom which the chairman now has and always has had, throughout the period since the board was first established in 1933, to arrange the board's internal business as he sees fit. For example, it will be possible for all seven members of the enlarged board to sit on any reference

or appeal if, in the judgment of the chairman, the importance of that appeal or reference justifies such a procedure.
The proposed bill will provide also for minor and consequential amendments flowing from the proposal to increase the membership of the board and to adopt a panel system. These consequential amendments relate to such matters as the designation of the persons to preside at sittings of panels, revision of some of the provisions relating to the powers and functions which may be exercised by the chairman, vice chairmen and members of the board, and a new provision authorizing each member of the board to administer oaths and take and receive affidavits, declarations and affirmations.

The tariff board has been of great service to this government and to governments that have preceded it. On the other hand, by reason of legislation recently introduced by this government, I think one might wonder whether in the future this tariff board will have the same jurisdiction, the same influence and the same importance as it has had in the past. Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have now the opprtunity to deal with this subject in detail. The fact is that the proposed enlargement of the personnel of the board is very necessary, it is urgently necessary, because of the very large backlog of work now awaiting consideration by the board. At the present time that backlog consists of no fewer than eight references, and 69 appeals. The chairman of the board, in urging an enlargement of the board so that it may make some progress with this very large backlog, has informed me that according to his present estimate it would not be possible for the board to deal completely with this backlog of business within a couple of years.
It is just as true in this area of the nation's business as it is in the courts, that justice delayed is justice denied. Persons who have important matters within the scope of either appeals or references to the tariff board are entitled to have their business transacted before that board with a reasonable measure of dispatch.
The case that has been cited by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale is a case in point. The reference, No. 131, concerning oilseeds, vegetable oils and related products has been directed to the tariff board by myself, as I indicated I would do in the supplementary budget speech of December 20 last. Unless there is an enlargement of the personnel of the board, and if the board is compelled to go on as presently constituted, with only one panel, it will be a very long time before this reference can be heard.
Persons in this country who have important matters to put before the board in the course of hearings of references or appeals should have these matters dealt with as expeditiously as possible. Under present circumstances these matters are being delayed.
I think it is high time this action was taken. Far from questioning the importance of the board, the course that the government has followed enlarges the importance of the board. The course that I indicated earlier this afternoon, in accordance with my supplementary budget speech on December 20, points out the intentions of the government in regard to the review of the Customs Tariff and the modernization of many of its provisions, which by present-day standards are quite antiquated and badly need to be modernized. Undoubtedly a very large volume of work awaits the board, not simply the

backlog to which I referred, but also further references and other business which will undoubtedly come before the board from time to time.
At the present time it is estimated that one reference alone will occupy the time of the board for two years. This is the major reference on the chemical items in the Customs Tariff. These hearings have already been proceeding for several months, but much remains of this major undertaking on the part of the board. As long as the board is compelled to continue sitting as only one panel, there is simply no hope of the board reducing the backlog of work; on the contrary, it is likely that the accumulation of work will increase rather than be reduced.
Therefore the resolution now before the committee is intended to bring aid and assistance to this important tariff board, to enable it to transact more expeditiously the appeals and references which it has to hear, all of them of very great importance and in every one of which all interests concerned are entitled to a reasonably expeditious hearing and transaction of their business.

The house in committee on Bill No. S-7, respecting Queen's University at Kingston- Mr. Macdonnell-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, this is a rather intriguing bill from an historical point of view. Am I to judge from the answers to questions made by the sponsor when the bill was given second reading that the sponsor gave a rather detailed account of the reasons for this rather unusual bill so far as the powers of the university are concerned when the bill was considered by the committee?

Yes. The counsel for the university stated those reasons at some length. He referred to a statement made by the dean of the law faculty at the university who explained that this particular measure had reference to questions of administrative organization and was therefore not transgressing the rule that education is a matter for the provincial government to deal with. This is a matter of administration which goes back to the original act of 1882 now being amended. I was sorry to find that there is apparently no record of any debate at the time of the passing of the original act in 1882. The information regarding the matter of administration was apparently given and accepted in 1882 at the time that the statute was passed.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the sponsor whether he has any vested or personal interest in this bill as a result of being a foi ner student at the university in question?

I have a personal but not vested interest, if I understand correctly the meaning of those words. I certainly have a personal interest in regard to the passage of this bill because I think it would be of help to the present administration of the university. I point out this is not a mandatory matter but a permissive one. We all believe in flexibility and I would suggest that the passage of this bill will lead to flexibility in the position of the trustees in regard to their action from time to time.
Would the sponsor agree that I was correct in suggesting a vested interest if I explained that the vested interest was as a result of the contribution this university has made to Canada generally?

Yes, I imagine that would be right. From my point of view the university has made a great contribution. I would repeat the old saying, "it pleases he and it don't hurt I." I do not think this change does anyone harm but will do a lot of good.

Mr. Chairman, I raised certain questions on second reading but regret to say that I was not able to attend at the meetings of the committee to hear the answers. I did notice in reading the bill and also from what the hon. gentleman has said that this legislation was passed in 1882. It occurred to me as a historian that in 1882 Sir John A. Macdonald was prime minister of this country and that the Tories at that time believed in a unitary state and centralized form of government which perhaps explains why the legislation was passed without question by the parliament at that time. I have heard that some Tories in different parts of this country take a rather different view today. I wondered if the hon. member had sought to advise his colleague, the hon. member for Roberval, in regard to this bill before its presentation or if the hon. member for Roberval had taken any interest in regard to it at any stage of the proceedings?
As far as I am concerned the answer is in the negative. I am sure that any opinion from the hon. member would be of great interest.

Mr. Chairman, in the explanatory note to this bill I find the following:
The present name, the Canadian General Council of the Boy Scouts Association, was established when this association was, in effect, a branch of the boy scouts association incorporated by royal charter in London, England, on January 4, 1912. Since that time the Canadian association has become an independent member of the international boy scout conference.
Then, it goes on to give reasons for changing the name. The question I wish to ask the sponsor of this bill is, how has this association functioned since the time it became an independent member of the international boy scout conference? How did it operate legally? Was it incorporated on a national basis, and were its reports made under its act to the appropriate federal official, or was it incorporated under provincial legislation and the reports made to the provincial officials? If the hon. member's research into the bill is sufficient, I would like him to explain to the committee how the organization operates in Canada in relation to the provinces and the federal government under a royal charter granted in Great Britain in 1912?

maintopic: THE CANADIAN GENERAL COUNCIL OP THE BOY SCOUTS ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Since that time the boy scouts association of Canada was incorporated in Canada under an act of this parliament, an act which happened to be amended last year and is now before the committee. In any event, for a good many years the boy scouts association has operated under the terms laid down by an act of this parliament.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN GENERAL COUNCIL OP THE BOY SCOUTS ASSOCIATION

20 to 25 men in grade construction for a period of about two months. Employment will be provided for 60 to 70 men in the actual laying of the ballast and the rails for another period of a month and a half. For a period of approximately three and a half months, therefore, employment will be provided for some^ thing in the order of 60 men.
As I have said, this new spur line will service a new gas extraction plant of the British American Oil Company at a place called Rimbey, where gas will be produced for the trans-Canada pipe line. There will be 326 million cubic feet of raw gas daily going into the pipe line. In addition to this, Mr. Speaker, there will be 68,000 gallons of propane; 98,000 gallons of butane; 325,000 gallons of pentanes plus and 233 long tons of elemental sulphur. This will result in a considerable amount of traffic. The propane will result in approximately 10 carloads per day, the butane approximately 17 carloads per day, the pentanes plus approximately 50 carloads per day and the sulphur about 5 carloads per day.
The movement of these products will provide employment for two railway men daily at the plant and will call for the addition of three train crews in the division in which the spur line will operate. If one considers there are about four men to a crew, one can see that the increase will cover about 12 men. In addition, a section crew of four men will be needed. During the construction period, therefore, an average of 60 men will be employed for about three and a half months and permanent employment will be provided for something in the neighbourhood of 25 years for about 18 men.
I would ask the house to give second reading to the bill as quickly as possible so that it could go to a committee and be reported back to the house without delay. This matter is of considerable importance to the district I represent, to the oil industry and the economy of Alberta as well as to the economy of Canada generally when we consider that the export of this amount of natural gas will do a great deal in helping to correct our imbalance of trade with our neighbour to the south.

In the past.

Tariff Board Act

The minister surely cannot take the position that because he is not on the tariff board he should refrain from giving, or he should not be asked to give the house statistical information that will enable hon. members of this house, to determine whether or not the recommendation for an increase in the personnel of the tariff board should be acquiesced in.
That is the situation. I think the minister is taking an impossible position for any minister to take. I know the minister is an overburdened man. I realize that, but nevertheless the fact that he is overburdened does not relieve him of carrying out obligations which are his as a minister of the crown. Among those obligations is the one of answering questions that may assist hon. members in determining whether his proposals should be accepted. Does the minister take the position that this information should not be given to the committee? No one is asking him to sit down with pencil and paper and determine how many cases are of this kind or of that. All we are asking is that his parliamentary secretary, for instance, now leave the chamber, go to the telephone and ascertain from the registrar of the board what are the facts.
The problem is not any more difficult than that, and yet the minister sits there in his arrogance today and refuses to give us this information.
Surely the minister is going to get this information for us.
How can he? If the hon. member stayed in his seat he might get the information.

The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton who has just made a speech from his seat is an old member of this house who sat on this side of the house in the days when some of his friends at least did a lot of talking, and none more loudly than the present Minister of Finance, about the right of members of parliament to information and the right of members of parliament to speak.
Order.

There was no point of order from the other side then; they had all the chances to speak that they could possibly desire.

Tariff Board Act
And there were no flags.

We are being asked to vote the people's money; that is what we are being asked to do, to vote the taxpayers' money to increase the size of this board, and we seek to get some information, which ought to have been forthcoming in the first place, about the scope of the work the board now has. We are not speculating about its future work; we are talking about its present work. As my hon. friend from Essex East just said, the parliamentary secretary could earn a bit of his salary by going and telephoning to the board. We are not being unreasonable. If the minister had to do the counting himself we perhaps might have some doubts about it but, as the hon. member for Essex East has said, we are not asking the minister to do the counting himself; we would not think of asking him to do it. We are simply asking him to ask the board for the information and to give it to parliament whose servant he is supposed to be. This seems to be the hardest lesson for him to learn.
This is matter of great importance. I hope the minister is going to deal with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, of course, Mr. Chairman. However, the minister is not going to undertake to supply information until he knows that the information is available and in existence. Until I know it is in existence and available I do not think any hon. member should ask me to undertake to submit it. I hope I have made myself clear, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member has asked me to make inquiry. I will ascertain if the information is in existence and available.

The minister has made a concession which up until now he was reluctant to make. He has now undertaken to ascertain whether or not this statistical information is available. We thank the minister for this very generous attitude with regard to trying to supply parliament with information which we had presumed, of

course, was already in the minister's mind, when he decided to make this particular recommendation to his colleagues in the government and to parliament. I say that because I would think that the minister could not possibly determine whether the tariff board should be increased from five to seven members, unless he had some appreciation not of what the situation is likely going to be in the future in this context but of what the statistical record is to date with regard to this type of case that has come before the tariff board.
The minister, obviously stung by the question of the hon. member for Welland, now realizes the most unfortunate position in which he has allowed himself to be placed. While we have been urging the production of this information, the country should know what the attitude of the Minister of Finance is regarding this question. We have not asked merely what in the minister's opinion is likely to be the number of cases in the future-
Why would you not ask that?

-but rather what is the approximate number of cases of this type that the board has been engaged in considering up to now. The answer to that question certainly would dispel even the argument of the hon. member for Assiniboia who, without any rhyme or reason, said he was going to oppose the bill.
While we have been asking and are asking now for this information, what does the minister do? He has before him two very able officials. On his right is his parliamentary secretary. All around him in the house are many hon. members of the Conservative party who complain that they have not got enough to do. Surely between the officials, the parliamentary secretary and the hon. members who sit behind the minister, a telephone call could have been made to the registrar of the tariff board to ascertain how many cases of this type they have dealt with in the past. That information is available and has already been given to the house on other occasions.
Why don't you call them?

The hon. member for York-Scarborough says, "Why don't you call him?". Why does the hon. member for Essex East, the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, the hon. member for Ke-nora-Rainy River, the hon. member for Welland, not leave the house and go to the telephone booth and therefore provide that the data which the opposition should give to a measure such as this? That is the attitude

of hon. members of the Conservative party. This simple example indicates their disregard for parliament.
Yes, teacher.

The hon. member, who sits in his seat in the back row and whose only contribution is by way of interventions from his seat, says, "yes teacher". We are dealing now with an important principle, one that used to engage the attention of the Prime Minister when he was the private hon. member for Prince Albert, and later when he was the leader of the opposition. We asked the Minister of Finance to give us some information which he refused to give and with regard to which he said later that he would be glad to look into the matter and at some later date, if the information is available, he would give it to the house. That is the attitude of the government, and I regret that the Minister of Finance should be the instrument in this particular instance of the government's insolence and arrogance.

Mr. Chairman, I think the request that has been made is a very reasonable one. I do not understand why the Minister of Finance tried to evade the question or why he should tell the committee that unless the information is available he is not going to have the necessary research done that will disclose the information. On the request of hon. members of this house surely the minister should have a search made of the applications before the board to find out how many are class or kind appeals.
It is interesting to note that the hon. member for Essex East was relatively quiet this afternoon until recently and that he has made it clear that he and the other hon. members of his party support the resolution. They say now that they have not enough information and they want more. They say that we have pre-judged the matter. They have pre-judged it because they now admit that they came into the committee without adequate information. Now, in a great storm of indignation, they are telling the minister to produce the information because they need it but they have already said that no matter what information may disclose they are tying themselves in with the government and are voting for a two-panel system even though they do not know whether it is needed or what the present situation is.
They go on to say that they are not asking the minister to make an estimate of the number of cases in the future. The minister must have made an estimate of the work that will come before the board in the future because surely the legislation that is before the committee is based on that estimate. I suggest that class or kind cases are likely
Fire Losses Replacement Account Act to constitute a very substantial portion of appeals and references to the board. With the sweeping change in the definition a deluge of appeals on this very point will come before the board in the future. Members of the Liberal party say they are against the change in the definition, the widening of the rule, and they have proved they are against it, but they are prepared to facilitate the evil consequences of widening the rule by voting for the minister's measure and without having the necessary information. I think this is an indication of complete irresponsibility on the part of the official opposition.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to reply in any detail to the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia. I spoke on the resolution and I think everybody knows that this is just one of perhaps five stages in which this type of proposal will be advanced. I spoke with some knowledge of the value of the tariff board. I spoke with some knowledge of the delays in decisions following the deliberations and studies of the tariff board. He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill No. C-47 is to make the provisions of the
2738	HOUSE OF
Fire Losses Replacement Account Act fire losses replacement account available, subject to the approval of the treasury board, to certain proprietary crown corporations in addition to government departments and certain designated agency crown corporations that may now be granted advances from it. The act, which is chapter 28 of the statutes of 1953-54, establishes a fire losses replacement account and authorizes the Minister of Finance, with the approval of the treasury board, to make advances from the account up to a maximum of $5 million at any time to restore, rebuild or repair property administered or controlled by departments and certain agency crown corporations that had been damaged or destroyed by fire. The purpose was to ensure that when a fire loss did occur and the replacement or repair of the property destroyed or damaged was urgently and immediately required, and there was not sufficient money available in the appropriation for the service suffering loss, authority and funds could be obtained to proceed with the repair or replacement without delay, on the understanding that the account would be recouped subsequently by charges to the appropriation for the service concerned.
At present, the account is available to, (a) government departments as defined in the Financial Administration Act, except those departments or portions thereof excluded by regulation, and (b) agency crown corporations named in schedule C to the Financial Administration Act and designated by regulation for the purposes of the act. Under (a), to which I have referred, only the director of the soldier settlement and the director of the Veterans' Land Act have been excluded, while under (b), all agency crown corporations except the national harbours board have been designated. I may say that the national harbours board has its own self-insurance fund.
The proposed amendment would provide that proprietary crown corporations, such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which are dependent upon parliamentary appropriations for the financing of their capital programs, might conform to government general policy of underwriting its own fire loss risks, and be able to deal expeditiously with the repair or replacement of property damaged or destroyed by fire by drawing accountable and reimbursable advances from the account. It is urgent that this provision be made since such agencies as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have no recourse except to the Department of Finance appropriation for miscellaneous minor or unforeseen expenses, which could prove seriously inadequate if a major fire loss occurred.


The bill, Mr. Speaker, is a short one consisting of changes in only two sections of the act.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few brief remarks on this bill. I would not for a moment presume to make a lengthy analysis of its terms and import.
I listened with interest to the minister's detailed, and I thought quite thorough statement on the purpose and intent of the bill. It is a measure that covers, shall I say, the technical aspects of the administration of insurance in Canada, which to many of us sound as dry as dust. But it is a very important bill, related to the proper administration of something over $9 billion worth of investment in this country, investment upon which millions of Canadians depend at least for a measure of security in various respects.
I have had but a short time to glance through the bill. I must say that life in this parliament provides insufficient time to adequately study this type of bill. That is why we are very fortunate in being able to refer these matters to committees. However, in the short time I have had to read through the bill and, shall I say, digest it with my very slow-working mental digestion, as far as I can see the principle of the bill is to be found in clauses 12 to 16. These clauses make it possible for insurance companies to enlarge their investment powers, by providing a greater choice as to the type of investments in which they can indulge. I think
2756	HOUSE OF
Canadian and British Insurance Act that on the basis of experience, and particularly in view of our expanding and developing economy, that is a very wise and progressive provision.
As far as this group is concerned, I think it is quite safe to say that we hope this measure will increase Canadian savings, and that as the result of increasing Canadian savings it will increase Canadian ownership in these companies. As far as I can discover from reading the bill, that should occur as the result of these amendments.
As I said before, this is a technical, complicated piece of legislation. It requires specialists who actually understand this matter to explain and administer it. However, regardless of that it is a measure of great importance to millions of Canadians who find, through insurance of various types, a measure of security surrounding their daily lives and their future.
I am glad the minister has suggested that the bill should go to the banking and commerce committee where it should receive a thorough study. I agree with what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Ben-idickson) had to say. He said that not only should the committee listen to the superintendent of insurance and other capable officials of this government, but the committee should take this opportunity to hear evidence from those who are active in the administration of insurance companies and should be provided with an opportunity to question them.
I suggest there is no necessity for haste in dealing with an important, technical measure such as this. I suggest that the committee should take all the time needed to examine the officials, to hear evidence from those who administer or take part in the administration of insurance companies and to examine them. This is an extremely difficult and complicated question for any person to deal with if he is not closely connected with it from day to day. When the bill is reported to the house, I trust that the committee report will contain information that will be of value to us and will enable us to criticize constructively or to offer amendments to the various clauses of the bill with at least a greater understanding and a greater knowledge than is possible at the present time.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-71, respecting the civil service of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will not need to be reminded that last session the government introduced in the house a bill entitled "Bill No. C-77, a measure respecting the civil service of Canada to amend, revise and consolidate the Civil Service Act."
At that session the measure was not carried beyond first reading. The bill was distributed and the wish was expressed in the house that more time should be afforded for study of the bill and that it should not be pressed further at that session. That view commended itself to all sections of the house and accordingly the bill was not further proceeded with at the 1960 session. It is now my honour, Mr. Speaker, to bring forward a similar measure which is intended to have precisely the same purpose, namely to amend, revise and consolidate the Civil Service Act.
I stated briefly last year the background [DOT]of the measure at pages 5128 to 5130 of Hansard of June 20. I pointed out there that the measure:
-touches all aspects of the appointment, classification, tenure, rights and responsibilities of the civil
Civil Service Act
service of Canada, and the powers and duties of the independent civil service commission charged with responsibility in relation thereto.
I made comment upon the history of our legislation in this respect. May I refer briefly to what I said in that regard, as follows:
The present Civil Service Act enacted in 1918 is a landmark in Canadian history. It was a major advance over all the legislation which preceded it, including the acts of 1868, 1882, 1885 and 1908. At a stroke it placed the recruitment, promotion, classification and organization of the civil service of Canada beyond the reach of partisan political interference, and laid the foundation of what has come to be known as "the merit system". For many years the Civil Service Act has been the bulwark of this principle.
This principle, however, has not withstood all the tests to which it has been submitted. During world war II overriding legislation was adopted which permitted both the principles and the provisions of the act to be ignored and practices and procedures to grow up at variance with the letter of the law. During the post-war period it became increasingly clear that strict adherence to the provisions of the act prevented the civil service commission from giving such service to departments of government as it was required and indeed desired to give, particularly in the fields of organization and classification. In these latter fields the expansion of the country and the enlargement of the federal government's commitments posed special problems.
Since 1918 the functions of the civil service have undergone a transformation and proliferation. Its tasks have become infinitely more diverse, more complex, more technical and more specialized in keeping with the vast extension of the public business and the activities of government. More and more it has been recognized as essential to good government that Canada should maintain a public service of the highest competence in many fields and of unchallenged integrity.
Having sketched the background of the measure in these terms I refer to something that I am sure is fresh in the minds of all hon. members, namely the undertaking by the civil service commission itself of a review of the entire field of personnel administration in the public service with a view to the revision of the Civil Service Act. This request was first made to the commission by the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent in 1957, and that request was renewed to the commission when the present government took office later in that year. The report of the commission, which has taken its name from the chairman of the commission at that time, Mr. Heeney, was presented to the government and was tabled in parliament early in 1959. It attracted the widest interest across Canada and I am sure its contents have been studied by hon. members. I take advantage of the present occasion, Mr. Speaker, as I did on June 20, 1960, to pay a warm tribute to the members of the civil service commission, Mr. Heeney, Miss Addison and Mr. Pelletier, for the monumental task they performed in the writing of that

Civil Service Act
report. It takes its place among some of the reports of leading importance in recent Canadian. history.
I do not wish to detain the house by reviewing considerations that I am sure are fresh in the minds of hon. members from the discussion which was held some eight or nine months ago in this chamber. On that occasion, as I have indicated, I referred to the history of the act of 1918, and to the circumstances surrounding the decision to have the act thoroughly revised. It was after due consideration that the decision was taken not to proceed with the bill at that session, and in the course of that consideration and the discussions that were held in the chamber it was quite clear that all parties in the house recognized the measure as one of outstanding importance.
In introducing the present measure, Bill No. C-71, which closely resembles Bill No. C-77 of the last session, I propose to do no more than recapitulate very briefly some of the leading elements in the measure for the purpose of giving continuity to the present proceedings without traversing the same ground step by step.
The report of the civil service commissioners on personnel administration in the public service, known, as I have indicated, and fittingly, as the Heeney report, contains recommendations which have by and large been carried into the present measure so far as it was considered practicable to do so. There are two principal exceptions. The recommendation that government agencies at present outside the civil service should be brought within its compass and their personnel made subject to this bill has not been considered either practicable or desirable at this time, nor indeed is it likely to be acceptable to those who would be most directly affected, at any rate without a great deal of study and consideration.
In the second place, the recommendation of the Heeney report as to the application of the veterans preference has not been incorporated in the bill. The government has considered itself bound to maintain the privileges enjoyed by veterans with overseas active service to their credit which have existed in their favour during the past 15 years, and the recommendations in the Heeney report which would have abridged the veterans preference have not been carried into this measure, nor were they carried into Bill No. C-77 which was introduced at the last session.
I shall, Mr. Speaker, make only a brief allusion to those other features of the bill upon which I commented in more or less

detail on June 20, 1960. Perhaps I need do no more than enumerate them now:
1.	The limiting of the absolute authority of the civil service commission in matters affecting the organization of departments to that of an advisory role.
2.	The provision of greater flexibility in recruiting procedures in the sole discretion of the commission.
3.	The provision of the right of transfer into the civil service and the right to compete in promotional competitions in the civil service to be conferred on the public service as a whole.
4.	The establishment of the principle that an employee is paid as a matter of right rather than of grace, as has been the statutory rule hitherto.
5.	The establishment in the bill of the right to appeal from administrative decisions of departments and in an extended number of situations to the commission itself. In this respect there were some misapprehensions evidenced in the discussion of the measure last year. I hope these misapprehensions have since been removed and that it is now clearly understood by all hon. members who participated in the discussion at the last session that the appeals are not, as one of them thought, to a body outside the commission but will be appeals to appeal boards appointed by the commission and acting under the authority of the commission.
6.	The commission is also authorized to give a preference in selection, in cases wherever in its opinion effective service to the public requires it, to those who are skilled in the use of both the English and French languages.
I have no doubt that all hon. members have familiarized themselves with the terms of the earlier bill and this earlier study will unquestionably be of benefit to the select committee to which it is proposed that the present bill shall be referred after second reading.
Perhaps I might say a word briefly about changes introduced in the present measure compared with Bill C-77. Most of the changes, and they are numerous, are minor and of administrative significance only. They were suggested in various quarters and were studied by the government during the months which have elapsed since the earlier bill was introduced in June, 1960. I shall not dwell on these minor amendments.
There are, however, two changes which are matters of policy and to which the attention of the house might well be drawn. These give a clear indication of the spirit in which the government has considered the measure and the representations which were made to the government concerning it. A good deal

of publicity was given to the views of the civil service staff associations concerning the terms of clause 7 of the 1960 bill, C-77. That clause established in statutory form for the first time in our history recognition of the proposition that consultation should take place between representatives of the government and the commission and representatives of the staff associations on questions of pay and conditions of work. This clause was criticized on the ground that it reserved to the Minister of Finance and the civil service commission the right to initiate such discussions and that the right to initiate these discussions was not extended to the staff associations.
I should have thought that it would be accepted that no government of Canada would deny to the representatives of the civil service staff associations the right to initiate such discussions or that it would have been considered necessary to make statutory provision that on such initiation by the representatives of the civil service staff associations the government or the civil service commission, as the case might be, would sit down and discuss these matters with them. In this regard it is well to bear in mind, I think, that in the United Kingdom the system of Whitley councils, which is frequently referred to as a model in these matters of relationship between the government as employer and civil servants as employees, rests on no legislation at all. Therefore, one may ask if it is strictly necessary to dot all the i's and cross all the t's in a situation of this kind.
However, Mr. Speaker, the present measure is intended to remove all doubts in this regard. Unity of purpose and good faith are taken for granted on the part of both parties by the government in the drafting of the present measure, and it is as an earnest of this good faith and, I believe, unity of purpose that in the present measure clear provision has been introduced to provide recognition of the right of the staff associations to initiate discussions with either the government or the commission on the subjects I have mentioned.
The other major change relates to the definition of what are known as the prevailing rates group of government employees in the manipulative trades and occupations traditionally outside the classified civil service. Here it appeared that the definition might open the door to the enlargement of this group by the process of excluding certain classes from the civil service itself, without any control being exercised by the civil service commission. Accordingly, the bill has been drawn to make it clear that this was not the intention of the government
Civil Service Act
and to make it equally clear that action in relation to prevailing rates employees cannot be taken without a recommendation to such effect proceeding in the first place from the civil service commission itself. I wish to make it quite clear that there can be no suggestion whatever of taking outside the civil service those who come within the category of prevailing rates employees unless the matter is commenced by a recommendation from the civil service commission itself.
I do not propose, nor is this the time, to enlarge further upon the contents of the bill. I thought it fitting to refer in a general way to what I said on June 20 last and to indicate briefly and in outline the points on which the present measure differs from its predecessor. It may, however, be appropriate to repeat that the general purpose of the present measure is to reaffirm the principle of the merit system, to safeguard the independence of the civil service commission and of the service itself within the compass of legislation designed to meet the many administrative problems which have arisen in the course of the life of the act of 1918, without permitting any compromise of the principles for which the act has stood and which have earned universal approbation for more than 40 years in this land and beyond our shores.
It will be recalled by hon. members that at the 1960 session a special committee was appointed by the house for the purpose, as originally intended, of studying both Bill No. C-77 and the kindred bill to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act. The committee was set up and the bill to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act was referred to it. However, Bill No. C-77 did not reach the point of second reading and consequently was not referred to that committee. May I say of that committee that it was an excellent committee and it did very useful work in relation to the superannuation act amendments.
If it were to meet with the approval of the house I would propose, at the appropriate time, to move the reappointment of a similar committee. It was not a large committee. It was a committee of very suitable size for the task that was entrusted to it. I have placed on Votes and Proceedings of the house today, a notice of motion that a special committee be appointed to consider Bill No. C-71, an act respecting the civil service, with power to send for persons, papers and records and to report from time to time; that the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable or necessary; that the committee consist of 15 members to be designated by the house, and so on.

Civil Service Act
A committee of this size I think will be regarded by the house as appropriate for the type of intensive study that will be called for in relation to this measure. I will say no more about the importance of the measure. I think that importance was widely recognized in all parts of the house last year. Both as to its subject matter and as to the physical size of the bill, undoubtedly this measure will be a major piece of legislation and, perhaps in terms of size, the largest government measure to be before the house at this session.
It is in no perfunctory sense that I say the civil service of Canada holds a position of the highest respect, not only in the eyes of this country and this parliament but indeed its position and its prestige have been recognized in other countries as well. It is the senior element of the public service of this country that is best known in other countries. Our senior civil servants come frequently into contact with the senior civil servants of other countries, more particularly the countries of the commonwealth. One cannot attend these international meetings, particularly commonwealth meetings, without being frequently impressed with the high regard in which our civil servants are held in these other countries.
Last year I made mention of the increasing complexity of government and the burden which that increasing complexity casts upon the civil service. This has meant that our civil service, while expanding in numbers as it has over the last 20 years, has had to become infinitely more diverse, more technical and more specialized in keeping with the very great expansion of the duties cast upon it. It must be a civil service of the highest competence in order to discharge the great variety of tasks that fall upon it.
The first requisite of the civil service at all times must be unimpeachable integrity. While of course in a civil service as large as ours there will be, from time to time, derelictions I think it is a matter of very great satisfaction to all parties in this parliament that these cases are very rare indeed in relation to the very large numbers of persons involved.
It has been, I think, a matter of satisfaction to this parliament to have taken important, and may I say notable, steps to improve the conditions of the civil service. Within the past year, parliament has made it possible to provide substantial increases in salaries. Within the past year, the medical-surgical benefits have been introduced throughout the civil service. The amendments to the superannuation act which this parliament enacted at the 1960 session likewise brought very considerable benefits to the civil service and repaired situations that were calling for remedy. This present parliament also provided increases in superannuation benefits for those civil servants who had retired before the present parliament was elected. Those, Mr. Speaker, are the expressions on the part of this parliament of its due appreciation, in the name of the Canadian people, of the outstanding services rendered to this Canadian nation by the civil service of this country.

Has the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) ascertained whether any parliamentary committee has recommended that crown companies should follow the procedure generally laid down for other sections of government administration? I think this is a very desirable policy. I recall at one time being associated with the minister in a committee in
Fire Losses Replacement Account Act which this matter came up. I think the procedure in relation to crown companies should take the same form. This risk should be borne by the government on a national, overall basis, without payment to any intermediates such as agents or representatives of the normal insurance companies.
I did indicate to the minister before five o'clock that I wondered under what authority 

although I did not question that the authority existed-the public accounts for the year ended March 31, 1960, contained a complete blank in so far as a dollar and cent item was concerned under this fire losses replacement account. I wonder whether the minister would answer this question and relate it to recent years.
I am sure the minister understands that I am concerned about the looseness in the estimates for individual departments which suffer fire losses. Perhaps the minister will tell me whether I am right or wrong in regard to this question. Was the $5 million fund created under this enactment for the purposes of making it possible for departments to go ahead without delay in the event of a fire loss, in the absence of authority from parliament?
It occurs to me when I see a "nil" item in the public accounts, such as there was for last year, that perhaps the estimates granted to each department are just not as tight and close as the minister boasts in so many public speeches, when he says that never before has treasury board been so strict in its administration and authority over the various departments. I know that fire losses have been incurred by a number of departments and I have available the reports of the dominion fire commissioner.
I find that this provision was legislated in 1953-54. It was enacted to provide departments with a fund so that they could go ahead, if necessary, with construction rapidly after incurring a fire loss, when parliament could not vote the sum necessary to replace that loss. If last year no department of government required assistance under this legislation from this fund, either on a temporary basis or on a basis longer than the fiscal year, I wonder whether some of these remarks of the minister are valid, that there are under this government less lapses in expenditure estimates than there have been in any other government.
I think that in fact there must yet be looseness in the departments, if during the course of the fiscal year last reported upon by the auditor general, no money was needed for this particular provision. In other words, I suggest there were lapses. There was an excess fund in every department when a fire occurred so that they either replaced

speechtext:
The effect of this bill, when adopted, will be to make it possible to bring within the benefit of the fire losses replacement account the proprietary crown corporations listed in schedule D to the Financial Administration Act. Up to the present time, so far as the crown agency corporations are concerned, the benefit applied to those in schedule C to the Financial Administration Act. The effect of the amendments in the present bill will be to bring the proprietary crown corporations such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, within the benefit of the fund. That being the case, it will be possible for these corporations, acting on the same principle that the government follows in relation to carrying the risk of fire losses on its own property, to have recourse to the fund at any time subject to the approval of treasury board, in the event of loss through fire.
While I am on my feet I perhaps might deal with the point raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River this afternoon in relation to the public accounts. He drew attention to page A-21 of the public accounts for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1960 and commented that the accounts showed no monetary figure against the fire losses replacement account. The answer to the hon. gentleman is that the fire losses replacement account is not an account in the ordinarily accepted sense. The fact is that no funds accrue to it. The fund has $5 million provided for it under section 8 of the Fire Losses Replacement Account Act, chapter 28 of the statutes of 1953-54. This, under section 5 of the act, is an account in the consolidated revenue fund. Therefore the answer briefly is that the $5 million is not a fund in the ordinarily accepted sense of the term. It is really a limiting authority as will be seen when regard is had to the provisions of section 8 of the main act. Thus, if an advance is made at any time during the year, it remains against


that account until it is repaid by an appropriation within the same current year, as required by the act.

He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. S-5, an act to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act is in a sense associated with the bill which is next to follow according to the announcement made last night by the leader of the house, namely Bill No. S-6, an act to amend the Foreign Insurance Companies Act. While we of course do not attempt to discuss two measures at the same time or in the same debate, I think it may be said and understood by all hon. members that while the first of the two bills covers a wider area than the second, the points that are raised for discussion are similar.


At the conclusion of the debate on second reading, if it pleases the house to give the bill second reading, I shall propose that the same course be followed with respect to both bills, namely that they be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce. The superintendent of insurance, Mr. Kenneth MacGregor, will be available to that committee to offer such testimony concerning the details of both measures as the members of the committee may desire.
These bills, I may point out, have already been passed by the other place and were carefully reviewed there particularly at the committee stage. There is, of course, much in both bills that is highly technical. Our insurance legislation has not been comprehensively revised at regular intervals. The last major revision of our insurance legislation took place in 1950 but, as I shall point out later in my remarks, there have been three amendments since that time. The revision embodied in the bill now under debate is one that has been sought by the insurance companies themselves which are governed by it. There are important changes proposed to the insurance legislation in these bills. Perhaps the most important consists of the provisions for enlarging and broadening the powers of investment of the companies. Indeed, it may be said that the purpose of the measure in this regard is to enlarge the freedom and flexibility of the insurance companies in relation to their investing powers. An important new provision is introduced in relation to variable annuities or contracts. So much by way of introduction.
There are very few persons in Canada whose lives or property are not affected, directly or indirectly, by insurance. The protection afforded by insurance is interwoven throughout the fabric of our modern mode of living and our economic structure. Insurance eliminates or reduces risks that would otherwise cause great distress or disaster. Insurance provides a bulwark against the hazards of accident, sickness, old age, death, fire and a multitude of other contingencies. It also stimulates savings, and some forms of insurance, especially life insurance, give rise to the accumulation of very large funds for investment. Consequently, the manner in which insurers carry on business in Canada and their investment policies, their stability and their solvency are of vital importance and concern to the entire Canadian public.
At present, there are 410 companies and 50 societies within the description of Canadian, British and foreign insurance companies and fraternal benefit societies registered under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act or the Foreign Insurance Companies Act to transact business under the supervision of

Canadian and British Insurance Act underlying this measure of freedom of investment was first adopted in 1948. It has since proved to be of great value in permitting companies to invest in new types of securities and experience has shown that this freedom has been carefully exercised.

speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? For the record, will he outline the type of assets that he is now referring to, namely those in the so-called basket?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVESTMENT AND OTHER POWERS
speechtext:
That will be evident, I think, as we proceed. We are speaking now of the investments which are permitted under the so-called "basket clause".
At the present time no company is using the existing freedom to the full extent permitted, but from time to time some companies have approached the present limit. It is now proposed to increase this limit to 5 per cent of a company's total assets.
Considering Canadian companies as a whole, since their total assets exceed $9 billion this means that such companies can make investments in real estate for the production of income, or in any kind of bonds not in default, or in stocks regardless of their dividend record, subject only to the wisdom of the companies themselves, up to a maximum amount of approximately $450 million. It is believed that the additional margin is justified on the grounds that the present freedom has been responsibly used and that the higher limit will permit a desirable participation by companies in new types of investments without the necessity of frequent amendments to the act to change the specific kinds of investment authorized and will permit the making of sound investments even though they do not meet the specific requirements of the various prescribed classes set forth in the act.
Changes are proposed in the provisions relating to real estate purchased for the production of income and leased back to a corporation that has a dividend record up to a prescribed standard, under a lease meeting certain minimum requirements. The act at present limits any particular investment of this type to half of 1 per cent of the book value of the total ledger assets of the company. It is proposed to increase this limit on any one parcel to 1 per cent of the company's total assets.
Furthermore, the act in its present form also limits the aggregate investments of a company in real estate for the production of income, whether of the particular kind just mentioned or any other kind, to 5 per cent of the book value of the total ledger assets of the company. It is proposed to raise this limit to 10 per cent of the company's total


assets. This type of investment, first authorized in 1948, has proved to be sound and profitable and particularly popular in a few companies that are approaching the present limit. A substantial degree of experience has been gained and it now appears that a higher limit can be adopted without weakening the general quality of the asset portfolios of the companies.
Another change relates to so-called equipment trust certificates. At present, companies may invest in equipment trust certificates issued by a trustee to finance the purchase of transportation equipment for a railway company incorporated in Canada or the United States and secured by such equipment. It is proposed to extend this provision to include transportation equipment for use on public highways. Equipment trust certificates have generally proved to be of high quality in both Canada and the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVESTMENT AND OTHER POWERS
speechtext:
No, I said transportation equipment for use on public highways.
It is proposed to authorize, as a new specific class of investment, the guaranteed investment certificates issued by Canadian trust companies, either federal or provincial, where such companies have a dividend record as good as the dividend record required to make the debentures of any other kind of company qualify as eligible investments.
Several other minor changes respecting investments are dealt with in the bills but their purposes are, I think, apparent from the explanatory notes printed in the bills.
Leaving the subject of investment powers, may I now touch upon a matter relating to the corporate powers of insurance companies in the pension and annuity field as well as the investment of funds arising under certain kinds of pension and annuity schemes.
Life insurance companies transacting business in Canada have expressed the desire, through representations made by the Canadian life insurance officers association, to make group contracts for the financing of employer-employee pension plans in such terms as to result in the contract holder receiving the full benefit or burden of investment gains or losses. Under such contracts, there would be no guarantee of investment return and the obligations of the insurance company would, in general, rise or fall with a rise or fall in the market value of the securities earmarked for contracts of this kind. For such contracts also, the companies wish to have greater freedom of investment than is now permitted under the

present legislation. It is well known that many employers prefer to see their pension funds invested in common stocks to a greater extent than the 15 per cent limit applicable to insurance funds as a whole and have set up trust funds for this purpose.
At present, Canadian life insurance companies have the corporate power to issue "annuities of all kinds", and to make contracts of "insurance providing for the establishment, accumulation and payment of sinking, redemption, accumulation, renewal or endowment funds". These companies thus have the corporate power to make such contracts provided there is some element of insurance in them but the act is not clear how such contracts should be dealt with in the accounts of the company. It is also doubtful whether this type of contract could be used to any appreciable extent within the present limitations on investments in common stocks applying to the life insurance funds of the company generally. So-called variable annuities, involving annuity payments varying from time to time in accordance with the investment results of a fund invested substantially or wholly in common stocks, fall in this same general category and since companies have the power to issue annuities of all kinds, they have the power to issue variable annuities, although few companies have yet expressed much interest in them.
If companies begin to issue contracts of the general kind to which I have just referred, under which the obligations to the policyholder vary with the market value of the investments held for the benefit of such contracts, it is of the utmost importance that such contracts should be dealt with in a manner completely separate from the normal life insurance business of the company.
It is therefore proposed to amend section 81 of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act so that if any such contracts are made by Canadian companies-and this would include so-called variable annuities- they shall be dealt with in a separate fund Dr funds and the assets belonging to any such fund or funds shall be segregated from the other assets of the company. Similar proposals respecting British insurance companies will be found in this bill and in the other bill. It is also proposed that the investments in any such separate fund be relieved from the existing limitations on the proportion that may be invested in common stocks or in real estate for the production of income. Investments would not, however, be relieved from the usual requirements with respect to kind and quality.
In this connection, I might mention that there is not complete unanimity amongst
Canadian and British Insurance Act the companies concerning the desirability of offering contracts of this general kind. Views have been expressed to the effect that life insurance companies should refrain from issuing any type of policy which does not provide benefits of guaranteed amount, lest unfavourable variations resulting from a fall in the value of the investments might detract from the public confidence now placed in the life insurance companies, a confidence that has been built up on the strength of guaranteed benefits.
To give effect to this view would require a narrowing of corporate powers at present enjoyed by Canadian life insurance companies. This would scarcely seem appropriate having regard to the fact that this view is seemingly held in a very few companies only, that provincially incorporated companies are already transacting this kind of business, that British companies apparently have the necessary power to do so, and that many United States companies are acquiring powers of this kind.
Instead, as I have already mentioned, the course proposed is to require separate funds and separate assets with, of course, separate accounting for such business in order to keep it quite separate from the regular life insurance and annuity business of the company. If life insurance companies are careful to explain the different nature of this kind of contract when it is made, the possibility of misunderstanding should be reduced, if not eliminated; and the availability of this kind of contract will enable the companies to meet a strong demand from various segments of the public to have funds arising under pension plans invested to a greater degree in equities than is otherwise permitted. Although no specific requirement is proposed at this time concerning the proportion of any such fund that should be invested in Canadian securities, it is taken for granted that where the fund is held for the benefit of policyholders in Canada it will be invested mainly, if not wholly, in Canadian securities, including Canadian equities.
I turn now to another field in which life insurance companies have for many years been quite active. I refer to personal accident and sickness insurance.
At present, a Canadian life insurance company is permitted to transact classes of insurance other than life insurance if it has the charter power to do so or acquires the necessary power in accordance with the provisions of the act. It is required, however, to maintain the funds, accounts and securities held in respect of its life insurance business in a manner completely separate and distinct from the funds, accounts and securities for

Canadian and British Insurance Act any other class of business. Up to date, the only other class of business of any importance is personal accident and sickness insurance.
If a Canadian life insurance company wishes to engage in personal accident and sickness insurance, it must establish a separate fund for that purpose and the act permits the transfer from the life insurance funds of an amount not exceeding 25 per cent of the surplus of the company or $100,000, whichever is less, in order to create any such fund. However, having regard for the size of the large life insurance companies and the enormous growth in personal accident and sickness business, particularly with respect to group insurance, the amounts so available are no longer considered adequate. Furthermore, the act now permits a transfer only for the creation of the separate fund. There are no means whereby further transfers can be made from the life insurance funds to the accident and sickness fund even if such transfers should be necessary to maintain the solvency of the latter fund.
It is therefore proposed that the present limitation on transfers be changed to permit transfers either to establish or maintain the fund and, in addition, that the limit on the amount of transfers be increased for the larger companies to 10 per cent of the surplus. This will still retain the advantages of a clear separation between these two kinds of business but at the same time will afford some degree of flexibility in sustaining the accident and sickness fund, if necessary, in times of adversity.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, it is desirable to revise and rearrange several sections of the present legislation for greater clarity, to adapt their provisions better to meet current conditions and to remove minor defects or anomalies. Also, there are a few provisions which have become obsolete and should be repealed. The changes proposed in these respects are indicated in the bills themselves, and can be further discussed in the committee on banking and commerce. I say nothing concerning the other bill to amend the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, except to indicate that the amendments are, in general, virtually identical.
The house has had the benefit, through its banking and commerce committee in times past, of opportunities for studying insurance legislation with the very competent and highly valued assistance of Mr. Kenneth MacGregor, the superintendent of insurance. I have no doubt that the review of our existing legislation offered by the two present measures will be of very great benefit to our legislative efforts in parliament.
